title: Advanced Hooks Patterns — useImperativeHandle, useDebugValue, and Custom Hook Architecture

subChunks.title: Advanced Hooks Patterns — useImperativeHandle, useDebugValue, and Custom Hook Architecture
subChunks.hookHtml: Most React developers know useState, useEffect, and useContext. The advanced hooks — useImperativeHandle, useDebugValue, forwardRef, and sophisticated custom hook patterns — are what separate component library authors from application developers. This lesson covers the hooks you need to build genuinely reusable, debuggable, and composable custom hook systems.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
forwardRef — exposing a ref to the parent

import { forwardRef, useRef } from 'react';

// A custom Input that exposes its DOM ref:
const Input = forwardRef(function Input({ label, ...props }, ref) {
  return (
    <div>
      <label>{label}</label>
      <input ref={ref} {...props} />
    </div>
  );
});

// Parent can now focus the input programmatically:
function Form() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  return (
    <div>
      <Input ref={inputRef} label="Quest Title" />
      <button onClick={() => inputRef.current.focus()}>
        Focus Input
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

useImperativeHandle — exposing a custom API via ref

Instead of exposing the raw DOM node, expose a controlled imperative API:

import { forwardRef, useImperativeHandle, useRef } from 'react';

const VideoPlayer = forwardRef(function VideoPlayer({ src }, ref) {
  const videoRef = useRef(null);

  // Expose only the API you want — not the whole DOM node:
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
    play: () => videoRef.current.play(),
    pause: () => videoRef.current.pause(),
    seek: (seconds) => {
      videoRef.current.currentTime = seconds;
    },
  }));

  return <video ref={videoRef} src={src} />;
});

// Parent uses the controlled API:
function App() {
  const playerRef = useRef(null);
  return (
    <div>
      <VideoPlayer ref={playerRef} src="/quest-tutorial.mp4" />
      <button onClick={() => playerRef.current.play()}>Play</button>
      <button onClick={() => playerRef.current.seek(30)}>Skip 30s</button>
    </div>
  );
}

useDebugValue — label custom hooks in DevTools

import { useDebugValue } from 'react';

function useOnlineStatus() {
  const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine);

  useEffect(() => {
    const handler = () => setIsOnline(navigator.onLine);
    window.addEventListener('online', handler);
    window.addEventListener('offline', handler);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener('online', handler);
      window.removeEventListener('offline', handler);
    };
  }, []);

  // Shows 'useOnlineStatus: Online' or 'Offline' in DevTools:
  useDebugValue(isOnline ? 'Online' : 'Offline');

  return isOnline;
}

// With a formatter function (lazy evaluation):
useDebugValue(user, user => user ? `Logged in as ${user.name}` : 'Logged out');

Custom hook architecture patterns

The factory pattern — creating hooks with shared configuration:

// Create a hook factory for API endpoints:
function createEntityHook(endpoint) {
  return function useEntity(id) {
    const [data, setData] = useState(null);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);

    useEffect(() => {
      setLoading(true);
      fetch(`${endpoint}/${id}`)
        .then(r => r.json())
        .then(setData)
        .finally(() => setLoading(false));
    }, [id]);

    return { data, loading };
  };
}

const useQuest = createEntityHook('/api/quests');
const useUser = createEntityHook('/api/users');
const useItem = createEntityHook('/api/items');

Composing custom hooks:

// useQuestBoard = useFetch + useLocalStorage + useOptimistic:
function useQuestBoard() {
  const { data: quests, refetch } = useFetch('/api/quests');
  const [savedFilters, setSavedFilters] = useLocalStorage('quest-filters', {});
  const { optimisticUpdate } = useOptimistic(quests);

  const acceptQuest = useCallback((questId) => {
    optimisticUpdate(q => q.id === questId ? { ...q, accepted: true } : q);
    return fetch(`/api/quests/${questId}/accept`, { method: 'POST' });
  }, [optimisticUpdate]);

  return { quests, savedFilters, setSavedFilters, acceptQuest };
}

Vex: "useImperativeHandle is the escape valve for imperative control. 90% of React is declarative — you describe the UI you want and React renders it. But media players, canvas animations, and third-party imperative libraries sometimes need direct method calls. useImperativeHandle lets you expose a controlled imperative API without leaking the whole DOM node."

storyBeats.text: A video player component needs to expose play/pause/seek controls to its parent — but not the entire DOM element. A custom hook system manages five interacting state slices. Vex reaches for forwardRef and useImperativeHandle.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: forwardRef passes a ref through a component to the underlying element. useImperativeHandle replaces what that ref points to — instead of exposing the raw DOM node, expose only the methods you want the parent to call. The hook factory pattern creates parameterised hooks for related resources. Compose hooks to build higher-level abstractions.

storyBeats.speaker: useImperativeHandle — controlled API

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build two advanced hook patterns:

  • A TextInput component that uses forwardRef + useImperativeHandle to expose a custom API with { focus, clear, getValue } methods — not the raw DOM input
  • A useCounter custom hook factory: createCounterHook(min, max, step) that returns a useCounter() hook respecting bounds. Add useDebugValue to show the current value in DevTools.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a useStateMachine hook that implements a finite state machine. It takes an initial state and a transitions map ({ [currentState]: { [eventName]: nextState } }) and returns { state, send, can } where send(event) transitions if valid and can(event) returns whether the transition is possible from the current state. Use it to model a quest lifecycle: available → accepted → inProgress → completed. Add useDebugValue showing the current state. Write the TypeScript types so invalid states and events are compile errors.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain forwardRef and useImperativeHandle — what problem does each solve, and why is useImperativeHandle preferable to exposing the raw DOM node in most cases? Then explain the hook factory pattern — what does it enable that a single custom hook doesn't? Finally, what does useDebugValue do and when should you add it?

options: Allows a parent component to pass a ref to a custom component, which can then attach it to a DOM element or expose it via useImperativeHandle
Forwards all props from parent to child automatically
Creates a ref that persists across component re-renders
Enables ref usage in function components that don't use hooks
questions.answer: Allows a parent component to pass a ref to a custom component, which can then attach it to a DOM element or expose it via useImperativeHandle
questions.explanation: By default, refs passed to custom components are ignored — you can only attach refs to DOM elements. forwardRef creates a component that receives the ref as a second argument (alongside props) and can pass it to an inner DOM element or use useImperativeHandle to expose a custom API.

options: Customises the value exposed via a ref — instead of the raw DOM node, you expose a controlled object with specific methods
Makes a component's ref work with both class and function components
Handles imperative code (side effects) before the component renders
Provides an imperative API for updating state without re-rendering
questions.answer: Customises the value exposed via a ref — instead of the raw DOM node, you expose a controlled object with specific methods
questions.explanation: useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ play, pause, seek })) replaces what ref.current points to. Instead of the full HTMLVideoElement with 100+ properties and methods, the parent only sees { play, pause, seek }. This is the principle of least exposure — give the caller only what they need.

questions.prompt: You have a `TextInput` component that uses forwardRef. A parent passes a ref and calls `ref.current.focus()`. With useImperativeHandle exposing `{ focus, clear }` — what does `ref.current` contain?
options: The object { focus, clear } returned by the useImperativeHandle callback — not the underlying HTMLInputElement
The HTMLInputElement — useImperativeHandle adds methods to it
questions.answer: The object { focus, clear } returned by the useImperativeHandle callback — not the underlying HTMLInputElement
questions.explanation: useImperativeHandle completely replaces what the ref exposes. ref.current is exactly the object returned by the callback: { focus: () => inputRef.current.focus(), clear: () => ... }. The underlying inputRef stays internal. The parent can only call focus and clear — nothing else about the input is accessible.

questions.prompt: When is the hook factory pattern (`createEntityHook(endpoint)`) more appropriate than writing individual hooks?
options: When multiple hooks share the same logic structure but differ in configuration — the factory eliminates duplication and ensures all hooks behave consistently
When performance is critical — factory hooks re-render less often
When the hooks need to share state with each other
When the hooks are used in class components
questions.answer: When multiple hooks share the same logic structure but differ in configuration — the factory eliminates duplication and ensures all hooks behave consistently
questions.explanation: If useQuest, useUser, and useItem all have identical fetch/loading/error logic differing only by endpoint, a factory eliminates the repetition. Bug fixes and improvements apply to all generated hooks automatically. It follows DRY while keeping each hook focused — useQuest doesn't know about useUser's endpoint.
